description: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects older leaves near the base of the plant, producing characteristic concentric target-like rings.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric target-board rings on lower leaves
Yellowing halo surrounding leaf lesions
Premature leaf drop leading to sunscald on tomato fruits
Sunken dark lesions at the stem base
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani surviving in crop residue or soil
Warm temperatures (24°C - 29°C) combined with leaf wetness or high humidity
Spores spread by wind, rain splashes, and gardening tools
management: Prune affected lower leaves to improve airflow and reduce fungal load
Apply protective copper-based or chlorothalonil fungicides at first sign of symptoms
Remove and burn infected plant residue post-harvest
prevention: Practice 3 to 4 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry
Apply organic mulch around plant bases to prevent rain splash from soil
external_references: USDA Agricultural Research Service - Solanaceous Crop Diseases
IPM - Integrated Pest Management Guidelines for Tomato Early Blight

description: Late blight is a devastating disease caused by Phytophthora infestans (an oomycete). It spreads rapidly in cool, wet weather and can destroy entire tomato crops within days if left unchecked.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked oily spots on leaf tips and margins
White fuzzy mold growth on undersides of leaves during humid conditions
Brown to black firm decay spots on tomato fruit surface
Rapid wilting and collapse of whole foliage stems
causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans spores carried over long distances by wind
Cool temperatures (15°C - 22°C) combined with high humidity (>90%) or dew
Infected volunteer tomato plants or potato tubers nearby
management: Destroy and destroy severely infected plants immediately to prevent field spread
Apply systemic bio-fungicides or targeted contact fungicides (mancozeb, copper octanoate)
Maintain adequate plant spacing to facilitate rapid canopy drying
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant hybrid tomato cultivars
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potatoes
Monitor local weather disease alerts and spray preventative bio-protectants
external_references: FAO International Plant Protection Convention Bulletin on Phytophthora
University Agricultural Extension Guide: Late Blight Control

description: Leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (syn. Cladosporium fulvum). It thrives primarily in greenhouse environments or high-density gardens with limited airflow.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth directly underneath yellow spots on leaf undersides
Old foliage turns brown, curls, and drops prematurely
causes: Fungal spores activated by relative humidity exceeding 85%
Stagnant air circulation in greenhouses or crowded garden beds
Warm indoor temperatures (20°C - 25°C)
management: Increase greenhouse ventilation using exhaust fans and open vents
Spray recommended sulfur or bio-based fungicide sprays
Remove heavily infected foliage from lower canopy
prevention: Maintain relative humidity below 85% in enclosed growing spaces
Select resistant tomato varieties carrying Cf-2 through Cf-9 resistance genes
Space plants generously to enable maximum airflow
external_references: Greenhouse Vegetable Crop Protection Handbook - Passalora fulva

description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It causes severe defoliation of tomato plants, reducing yield and quality of fruit due to exposure to direct sunlight.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (1.5-3mm) with dark brown borders and light gray centers
Tiny black specs (pycnidia fruiting bodies) visible in center of spots under magnification
Leaves turn yellow, dry up, and fall off from bottom to top
causes: Septoria lycopersici over-wintering on solanaceous weeds and crop debris
Frequent rains, heavy dews, and temperatures between 20°C - 25°C
Splashing water transferring fungal spores to lower leaves
management: Prune affected bottom foliage as soon as small spots appear
Apply protective fungicides containing copper or chlorothalonil
Clean tools with disinfectant after pruning diseased plants
prevention: Mulch soil around tomato plants with straw or plastic sheeting
Avoid overhead watering; use ground drip lines
Clean garden bed thoroughly at the end of each growing season
external_references: Plant Disease Journal - Septoria Lycopersici Management

description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny sap-sucking arachnids that feed on tomato leaves, causing stippling, discoloration, and fine webbing.
symptoms: Yellow or bronzed stippling dots across leaf surfaces
Fine silk webbing on leaf undersides and terminal shoots
Leaves turn brittle, dry out, and turn bronze-brown before dropping
causes: Hot, dry, and dusty weather conditions favoring rapid mite multiplication
Over-use of broad-spectrum insecticides killing natural mite predators
management: Spray undersides of leaves with strong streams of water to dislodge mites and destroy webs
Apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or horticultural oils
Introduce beneficial predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
prevention: Keep soil adequately moist and overhead misting during dry heat waves
Maintain border flora that harbors predatory insects
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization which creates succulent foliage favored by mites
external_references: Agricultural Entomology Extension - Spider Mite Control in Solanaceous Crops

description: Target spot is caused by Corynespora cassiicola. It attacks foliage and fruit, forming brown necrotic spots that resemble targets.
symptoms: Small double-ring brown spots expanding into target-like brown lesions
Chlorotic yellow halo around leaf spots
Pitted, sunken lesions on tomato fruit with dark centers
causes: Corynespora cassiicola fungus favored by warm, humid climate (20°C - 32°C)
Extended periods of leaf wetness and high rainfall
management: Apply registered fungicides such as azoxystrobin or copper compounds
Strip off lower infected leaves to minimize inoculum
prevention: Ensure proper crop spacing and weed management
Rotate tomatoes with non-host crops like corn or grasses
external_references: Tropical Plant Pathology Bulletin - Corynespora Target Spot

description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus is a viral disease transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting and leaf curling, leading to dramatic yield loss.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaf margins
Severe chlorosis (yellowing) between leaf veins
Stunted plant growth and failure of flowers to set fruit
Leathery and thick leaf texture
causes: Begomovirus infection transmitted by feeding whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
Presence of infected weed reservoirs near fields
management: Control whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps and neem oil sprays
Remove and rouge out virus-infected young plants immediately
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant cultivars (e.g., Ty-1 or Ty-3 resistance genes)
Use fine mesh insect screens in greenhouses to exclude whiteflies
Refrain from planting near old infested crops
external_references: Virology Journal - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus Epidemiology

description: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly stable tobamovirus that spreads mechanically through hands, tools, and infected seeds, causing mottled green and yellow leaf patterns.
symptoms: Alternating light and dark green mottled 'mosaic' pattern on leaves
Fern-like leaf distortion and stringy leaf blades
Internal browning and uneven ripening of fruit
causes: Mechanically transmitted Tobamovirus surviving on tools, stakes, and hands
Infected seeds or tobacco products handled by garden workers
management: No chemical cure exists for viral plant infections; rogue out infected plants
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling healthy plants
Disinfect garden tools in 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or bleach solution
prevention: Purchase certified virus-free seeds
Use resistant varieties with Tm-2 gene
Prohibit tobacco use near tomato gardens
external_references: International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses - Tobamovirus Profile

description: The leaf shows optimal health with deep green color, smooth vein structure, firm texture, and complete absence of spots, lesions, fungal growth, or pest infestation.
symptoms: Vibrant uniform green pigmentation
Intact leaf margins without burning or chlorosis
Strong turgid stem and leaf structure
causes: Balanced soil nutrients, appropriate sunlight exposure, and proper irrigation
management: Maintain current good cultural and agricultural practices
Regularly inspect leaves for early detection of potential pests
prevention: Continue balanced N-P-K fertilization and deep soil hydration
external_references: Standard Botanical Reference for Solanaceous Crops

description: Potato Early Blight is caused by Alternaria solani. It targets mature leaves, creating dark brown concentric ring spots that prematurely defoliate the crop and reduce tuber yield.
symptoms: Concentric ring dark brown spots on mature foliage
Yellow chlorotic tissue surrounding foliage spots
Sunken dry rot lesions on potato tubers
causes: Alternaria solani spores surviving in infected tuber debris and soil
High humidity and warm weather
management: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting at tuber initiation
Maintain optimal plant vigor with adequate nitrogen
prevention: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous species for at least 3 years
Destroy potato vines 2 weeks prior to harvest
external_references: Potato Association of America Handbook on Foliage Diseases

description: Potato Late Blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans. Historically famous for causing the Irish Potato Famine, it rapidly rots foliage and potato tubers.
symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions expanding rapidly across foliage
White cottony growth on underside of leaves under humid conditions
Reddish-brown dry rot extending into tuber flesh
causes: Phytophthora infestans sporangia spread by wind and rain
Cool temperatures (10°C - 20°C) and high humidity (>90%)
management: Apply systemic fungicides promptly upon detection
Kill vines completely before tuber harvest to prevent tuber contamination
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes
Hill up soil around potato plants to protect tubers from fungal spores
external_references: International Potato Center (CIP) - Late Blight Management

description: Healthy potato leaf with robust chlorophyll distribution, crisp margins, and no signs of bacterial wilt, blight, or pest damage.
symptoms: Uniform green foliage with firm venation
No spotting, wilting, or fungal growth
causes: Proper crop management, certified seed tubers, and optimal weather conditions
management: Continue standard irrigation and weed control
prevention: Regular scouting for potato beetle and foliage spot symptoms
external_references: Potato Agronomy Best Practices Manual

description: Corn Common Rust is caused by Puccinia sorghi. It produces powdery reddish-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Small, elongated cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across leaves
Pustules rupture to release powdery reddish-brown fungal spores
Leaves turn yellow and die prematurely if infection is severe
causes: Puccinia sorghi spores blown northward on wind currents from tropical regions
Cool to moderate temperatures (16°C - 23°C) and high relative humidity
management: Apply foliar fungicides if rust attacks upper canopy prior to silking stage
Fungicide treatment is rarely economical unless susceptible hybrids are grown
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrid varieties
Plant early in the season to avoid peak spore migration windows
external_references: Cereal Crop Disease Guide - Puccinia sorghi

description: Northern Corn Leaf Blight is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It creates large, cigar-shaped grayish-green lesions that reduce photosynthetic area.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions (2.5-15cm long) on leaves
Lesions start grayish-green and mature into tan or brown spots
Dark dusty spore masses inside lesions during wet weather
causes: Exserohilum turcicum fungus surviving in corn crop residue
Moderate temperatures (18°C - 27°C) and extended wet leaf periods
management: Apply foliar fungicides at silking if disease is present on ear leaves
Incorporate infected residue deep into soil after harvest
prevention: Plant NCLB-resistant corn hybrids with Ht genes
Rotate with non-host crops such as soybeans or alfalfa
external_references: Corn Disease Working Group - Northern Leaf Blight Advisory

description: Healthy maize leaf displaying vibrant green color, strong central midrib, and complete absence of rust pustules or blight lesions.
symptoms: Smooth green leaf blade without brown or yellow spots
Sturdy central midrib
causes: Adequate soil nitrogen, sufficient sunlight, and good drainage
management: Maintain side-dress nitrogen schedule and weed-free field borders
prevention: Standard crop rotation and certified seed usage
external_references: International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT)

description: Apple Scab is caused by Venturia inaequalis. It infects leaves and fruit, causing olive-green to black velvety spots that result in cracked, deformed apples.
symptoms: Olive-green to dull dark brown velvety spots on leaf surfaces
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely in mid-summer
Scabby, corky, black cracked spots on apple fruits
causes: Venturia inaequalis ascospores released from fallen overwintered leaves
Cool, rainy spring weather
management: Apply preventative fungicides (captan, myclobutanil) during bud break and bloom
Rake and burn fallen apple leaves in autumn
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Prima, Enterprise)
Prune canopy trees annually to promote internal sunlight and rapid drying
external_references: Tree Fruit Research Bulletin - Venturia inaequalis Management

description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects apple leaves (causing 'frog-eye' leaf spots), branches, and fruit (causing mummified black rotted apples).
symptoms: Small purple specks on leaves expanding into circular 'frog-eye' spots with purple margins
Black firm rot on fruit expanding in concentric rings
Sunken dark cankers on branches and limbs
causes: Botryosphaeria obtusa overwintering in mummified fruit, dead wood, and cankers
Warm weather (20°C - 27°C) accompanied by rain
management: Prune out dead wood, cankers, and fire blight strikes during winter dormancy
Remove all mummified apples remaining on trees or orchard floor
prevention: Apply copper sprays early in the season
Avoid wounding fruit or bark during harvest and pruning
external_references: Orchard Disease Management Manual - Black Rot

description: Healthy apple foliage exhibiting dark green color, firm serrated leaf edges, and absence of fungal leaf spots or rust marks.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaf canopy with clean serrated margins
No velvet spots, frog-eye rings, or deformation
causes: Proper orchard canopy management, dormant copper spraying, and good air drainage
management: Maintain annual dormant pruning and balanced micronutrient sprays
prevention: Routine orchard scouting and fallen leaf sanitation
external_references: Pomology & Tree Fruit Production Standard
